## Overview

Vignette 3 priced information about the current vegetation by assuming it was known
exactly. A manager does not get the vegetation; they get a survey, which costs money and
can be wrong. Whether to commission it is a decision in its own right, taken before the
grazing decision and informing it [@Runge2011]. This vignette builds that two-decision
problem from pieces with the open influence diagrams of
`CategoricalInfluenceDiagrams.jl`:

```text
 site                  monitoring                          grazing
 CurrentVegetation --> Survey (decision) -> SurveyResult --> the grazing diagram of vignette 3,
                       SurveyCost(Survey)                    its decision reading ClimateForecast,
                                                             Survey and SurveyResult
```

The boundary between the monitoring and the grazing component carries the true
vegetation, which drives the ecology, and the survey, which informs the manager. Only the
second is observed. The grazing component is written once; survey designs of different
accuracy and cost are compared by changing the monitoring component's numbers only.
Every composite is checked against the same problem built as one influence diagram.

## Setup

```{julia}
using EcologicalBayesianNetworks
using InfluenceDiagrams
using CategoricalInfluenceDiagrams
```

The numbers are those of the zoo's grazing diagram under the third valuation of
vignette 3: a benefit of 1000 for high biodiversity, and costs of 51, 25 and 0 for
excluding, reducing and maintaining grazing. Under it the decision is close enough to a
tie that the vegetation matters:

```{julia}
g = reference_grazing_id()
k = bind_utility(g, [:ConservationBenefit => [0.0, 1000.0],
                     :ManagementCost => [-51.0, -25.0, 0.0]])
informed = optimize(k).expected_utility
uninformed = optimize(without_information(k, :GrazingManagement, :CurrentVegetation)).expected_utility
(informed = informed, uninformed = uninformed, perfect_survey = informed - uninformed)
```

## Three components

The site holds the prior on the current vegetation and passes it on, hidden: it is the
state of the world, not something anyone has seen.

```{julia}
veg = [:sparse, :moderate, :dense]
site = Open(InfluenceDiagram(bayesnet(:CurrentVegetation => veg));
            outputs = [:CurrentVegetation])
println(site)
```

The monitoring component takes the vegetation as a hidden input. It holds the decision
`Survey` (survey or skip), with no information of its own; the survey result, which
reports a vegetation class when the survey is made and `none` otherwise; and the cost of
surveying. It passes on the vegetation, still hidden, and the decision and its result,
observed. `observed` flags each foot separately; here it names the two variables on the
output foot only.

```{julia}
results = [:sparse, :moderate, :dense, :none]
monitoring = Open(influence_diagram(:CurrentVegetation => veg, :Survey => [:survey, :skip],
                                    :SurveyResult => results;
                                    mechanisms = [:SurveyResult => (:CurrentVegetation, :Survey)],
                                    decisions = [:Survey => Symbol[]],
                                    utilities = [:SurveyCost => :Survey],
                                    closed = false);
                  inputs = [:CurrentVegetation],
                  outputs = [:CurrentVegetation, :Survey, :SurveyResult],
                  observed = (outputs = [:Survey, :SurveyResult],))
println(monitoring)
```

The grazing component is the grazing diagram of vignette 3 with the current vegetation,
the survey decision and its result as inputs. Its decision reads the forecast, as before,
and the survey and its result in place of the vegetation. It reads the survey decision as
well as the result because the composite must have no-forgetting: a later decision knows
what an earlier one chose. `Climate` is given a root mechanism explicitly, because with
`closed = false` a variable without one would be an input.

```{julia}
weather(x) = x => [:dry, :normal, :wet]
variables = [:CurrentVegetation => veg, :Survey => [:survey, :skip], :SurveyResult => results,
             weather(:Climate), weather(:ClimateForecast),
             :SoilMoisture => [:low, :medium, :high],
             :GrazingManagement => [:exclude, :reduce, :maintain],
             :GrazingPressure => [:low, :high], :Vegetation => veg,
             :HabitatQuality => [:poor, :good], :Occupancy => [:absent, :present],
             :Biodiversity => [:low, :high]]
ecology = [:ClimateForecast => :Climate, :SoilMoisture => :Climate,
           :GrazingPressure => :GrazingManagement,
           :Vegetation => (:SoilMoisture, :GrazingPressure, :CurrentVegetation),
           :HabitatQuality => :Vegetation, :Occupancy => :HabitatQuality,
           :Biodiversity => :Occupancy]
grazing_decision = :GrazingManagement => (:ClimateForecast, :Survey, :SurveyResult)
grazing_utilities = [:ConservationBenefit => :Biodiversity,
                     :ManagementCost => :GrazingManagement]
grazing = Open(influence_diagram(variables...;
                                 mechanisms = [:Climate => Symbol[]; ecology],
                                 decisions = [grazing_decision],
                                 utilities = grazing_utilities, closed = false);
               inputs = [:CurrentVegetation, :Survey, :SurveyResult],
               observed = (inputs = [:Survey, :SurveyResult],))
println(grazing)
```

## The manager cannot read the vegetation

The boundary says what the grazing decision may use. A grazing component whose decision
reads the vegetation itself is refused when it is opened with the vegetation hidden (rule 3
of the typed-interface rule):

```{julia}
reads_vegetation = influence_diagram(variables[1:3]..., variables[7];
                                     decisions = [:GrazingManagement => (:CurrentVegetation,
                                                                         :Survey, :SurveyResult)],
                                     closed = false)
try
    Open(reads_vegetation; inputs = [:CurrentVegetation, :Survey, :SurveyResult],
         observed = (inputs = [:Survey, :SurveyResult],))
catch e
    sprint(showerror, e)
end
```

Declaring the vegetation observed on the grazing side does not help, because the
monitoring component passes it on hidden, and the two sides of a boundary must agree:

```{julia}
try
    site ⋅ monitoring ⋅ Open(reads_vegetation;
                             inputs = [:CurrentVegetation, :Survey, :SurveyResult],
                             observed = (inputs = [:CurrentVegetation, :Survey, :SurveyResult],))
catch e
    sprint(showerror, e)
end
```

A decision that sees the true state has to be written in the monitoring component, as a
survey that is perfect, and then it is priced like any other survey.

## Composing and checking against one large diagram

The three components compose into a closed influence diagram with two decisions and three
utilities:

```{julia}
whole = site ⋅ monitoring ⋅ grazing
println(whole)
```

```{julia}
to_graphviz(apex(whole); states = false)
```

The same problem written as one influence diagram, with every arc stated at once, is the
oracle. Its apex is isomorphic to the composite's:

```{julia}
monolithic = influence_diagram(variables...;
                               mechanisms = [:SurveyResult => (:CurrentVegetation, :Survey);
                                             ecology],
                               decisions = [:Survey => Symbol[], grazing_decision],
                               utilities = [:SurveyCost => :Survey; grazing_utilities])
is_isomorphic(apex(whole), monolithic)
```

A survey design is its accuracy, the probability of reporting the true class (the two
wrong classes share the rest equally), and its cost. `design` binds the zoo's tables, the
survey's table and the utilities to the monolithic diagram, and reads off the kernels and
utilities that the composite takes by name:

```{julia}
function survey_table(accuracy)
    t = zeros(3, 2, 4)    # (CurrentVegetation, Survey, SurveyResult)
    for v in 1:3, r in 1:3
        t[v, 1, r] = r == v ? accuracy : (1 - accuracy) / 2
    end
    t[:, 2, 4] .= 1.0
    return t
end
chance = [:Climate, :ClimateForecast, :SoilMoisture, :CurrentVegetation, :GrazingPressure,
          :Vegetation, :HabitatQuality, :Occupancy, :Biodiversity]
function design(accuracy, cost)
    m = bind_cpt(InfluenceDiagramModel(monolithic),
                 Pair{Symbol,<:AbstractArray}[[x => cpt(kernel(k, x)) for x in chance];
                                              :SurveyResult => survey_table(accuracy)])
    m = bind_utility(m, [:SurveyCost => [-cost, 0.0], :ConservationBenefit => [0.0, 1000.0],
                         :ManagementCost => [-51.0, -25.0, 0.0]])
    kernels = Dict{Symbol,FiniteKernel}(x => kernel(m, x) for x in [chance; :SurveyResult])
    return m, kernels, Dict{Symbol,AbstractUtility}(bound_utilities(m))
end
nothing # hide
```

A field survey that is right four times in five and costs 0.2:

```{julia}
m, kernels, utilities = design(0.8, 0.2)
best = optimize(whole, kernels, utilities)
oracle = optimize(m)
(composite = best.expected_utility, monolithic = oracle.expected_utility,
 same_strategy = best.strategy == oracle.strategy,
 brute_force = expected_utility(m, best.strategy))
```

The last number is the expected utility of the composite's strategy by brute force over
the joint law of the monolithic model. The survey is commissioned:

```{julia}
policy_table(best.strategy[:Survey])
```

The grazing policy is a table over the forecast, the survey decision and the result. On
the surveyed slice, rows are the forecast (dry, normal, wet) and columns the reported
vegetation (sparse, moderate, dense, none); the `none` column is never reached once the
survey is made:

```{julia}
policy_table(best.strategy[:GrazingManagement])[:, 1, :]
```

It is the split vignette 3 found with the vegetation known, now acting on the report:
exclusion where the survey reports moderate vegetation, and where it reports sparse
vegetation under a wet forecast; reduction elsewhere.

## Pricing survey designs

The value of a survey design is what the composite earns with it, the survey made free,
minus what it earns without it. Changing the design changes one table and one utility of
the monitoring component; the grazing component and the composite are untouched:

```{julia}
value(accuracy) = optimize(whole, design(accuracy, 0.0)[2:3]...).expected_utility - uninformed
accuracies = [1 / 3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0]
[round(a; digits = 2) => round(value(a); digits = 3) for a in accuracies]
```

A survey that reports at random (accuracy one third) is worth nothing, and a perfect one
is worth exactly what vignette 3 found for knowing the vegetation. In between the value
falls below the straight line joining them: a survey right four times in five recovers
about 60% of the perfect-information value where the line would give 70%, and one right
three times in five under 30% where the line would give 40%. That is the number to set
against a quoted survey cost, not the perfect-information bound.

The value is also the break-even cost. Priced just below it the survey is commissioned,
and just above it it is not:

```{julia}
v8 = value(0.8)
[round(c; digits = 3) => policy_table(optimize(whole, design(0.8, c)[2:3]...).strategy[:Survey])
 for c in (v8 - 0.01, v8 + 0.01)]
```

## The survey decision in context

The monitoring component is open, so it has no expected utility of its own. It has one in
a context: the law the site induces on the vegetation, and the value that the grazing
component earns from each joint state of the vegetation, the survey choice and the
result. That value depends on the grazing policy, so the context is fixed by choosing one.
With the grazing policy of the composite's optimum, the monitoring component optimised in
context commissions the survey and attains the composite's optimum:

```{julia}
ν = boundary_law(site, kernels, utilities, Strategy())
grazing_value(τ) = continuation_value(grazing, kernels, utilities,
                                      Strategy(:GrazingManagement => τ))
informed_policy = best.strategy[:GrazingManagement]
with_informed = contextual_optimize(monitoring, kernels, utilities; prior = ν,
                                    continuation = grazing_value(informed_policy))
(survey = policy_table(with_informed.strategy[:Survey]),
 value = with_informed.expected_utility,
 matches_composite = with_informed.expected_utility ≈ best.expected_utility)
```

A survey is worth only what the manager does differently because of it. Take instead the
grazing policy that is optimal without a survey, which reads only the forecast, copied
across every survey result. It is read off the composite with the survey priced at 1, above
its value, where the survey is skipped and the result is always `none`. Against it the
survey earns nothing but its cost, and the monitoring component optimised in context skips
it:

```{julia}
skipped = optimize(whole, design(0.8, 1.0)[2:3]...)
forecast_only = policy_table(skipped.strategy[:GrazingManagement])[:, 2, 4]
ignoring = DeterministicPolicy(:GrazingManagement,
                               [FiniteAxis(:ClimateForecast, [:dry, :normal, :wet]),
                                FiniteAxis(:Survey, [:survey, :skip]),
                                FiniteAxis(:SurveyResult, results)],
                               FiniteAxis(:GrazingManagement, [:exclude, :reduce, :maintain]),
                               [forecast_only[f] for f in 1:3, s in 1:2, r in 1:4])
c_ignoring = grazing_value(ignoring)
with_ignoring = contextual_optimize(monitoring, kernels, utilities; prior = ν,
                                    continuation = c_ignoring)
surveyed_anyway = contextual_value(monitoring, kernels, utilities,
                                   Strategy(:Survey => ConstantPolicy(:survey));
                                   prior = ν, continuation = c_ignoring)
(survey = policy_table(with_ignoring.strategy[:Survey]),
 skip_value = with_ignoring.expected_utility, uninformed = uninformed,
 surveyed_anyway = surveyed_anyway, uninformed_minus_cost = uninformed - 0.2)
```

So the survey and the grazing policy cannot be settled one at a time. Valued against the
grazing policy chosen without it, a survey never pays and is never commissioned; valued
against the policy that uses it, it pays whenever it costs less than about 0.33. The
optimum of the composite is the best pair, which `optimize` finds on the closed composite,
and which the monitoring component attains in context only once the grazing policy that
goes with it is known.

## Summary

The decision to monitor was added to the grazing problem of vignette 3 as a component of
its own, between the site and the grazing diagram. The boundary carries the true
vegetation hidden and the survey observed, so the grazing decision can act only on what the
survey reports, and a component that tried to read the vegetation was refused. The
composite is isomorphic to the problem written as one diagram and agrees with it on the
optimum, the strategy and a brute-force evaluation. Survey designs were compared by
changing the monitoring component's numbers alone; an 80% accurate survey is worth about 60% of perfect
information, and that, not the perfect-information bound, is what its price should be
compared with. Optimised in the
context the site and the grazing component induce, the monitoring component commissions
the survey when the grazing policy uses its result, and skips it when the policy ignores
the result, which is why the two decisions are optimised together.
